I give myself ten minutes before a first call, and I look for three things, always in the same order. First, who they sell to. Not what they sell, who they sell to, because that tells me whether we have anything in common. Second, what changed in the last year. A new office, a new product, a new person in a senior role, anything that gives me a reason to be curious. Third, the person who will be on the call, because a partner manager and an engineer need completely different conversations. I stopped reading product pages years ago. Every product page in this industry says the same four things, and none of them tell me anything about that particular company. And here is the part people get wrong: I never recite what I found. Nothing kills a first call faster than a stranger reading your own website back to you. I turn one fact into one question, and then I stop talking.

There is a sentence at the top of our own company page, and I want to be honest about it: nobody has ever said that sentence out loud. Not me, not the sales team, not the person who wrote it, and a lawyer and a marketing agency wrote it together, which explains a lot. When I describe the same company at a dinner, it comes out completely differently. I say we work with factories that cannot tell you on Friday what they produced on Monday, and everybody at the table understands immediately, because everybody has worked somewhere that was a bit like that. So my advice, when you read a company page before a call, is simple. Read it for the facts and never for the words. Take the numbers, take the names, take the markets and the dates. Then throw the adjectives away, because they were not written to tell you anything.
